notes.made: Credited to Mark King, Mike Lindup, Phil Gould, Boon Gould and Wally Badarou, it started with Lindup playing the rising opening line on piano and the whole band building on it. Boon Gould brought in new verse lyrics to replace the ones his brother Phil had written, which annoyed Phil. Badarou, the Paris-born keyboardist from the Compass Point house band, co-produced World Machine with the band and played keyboards and Synclavier; Julian Mendelsohn recorded and mixed it.
notes.context: After True Colours disappointed, Polydor wanted a hit, and this was it: released 13 September 1985, number 6 in the UK, number 7 on the Hot 100, their only American top 10. World Machine went to 3 and stayed on the UK chart for 72 weeks. Stuart Orme's video casts King as a dark clown magician breaking up the others' relationships, all with Cherie Lunghi.

listen_for.note: Lindup's rising piano line, the seed of the whole song.
Boon Gould's lyrics, the rewrite that Lindup said lifted the song.

leads_to.title: Chief Inspector
leads_to.why: Badarou's own synth-funk instrumental from Echoes; it charted at 46 in the UK in October 1985, the same autumn as this single.

notes.unverified: No session-level source for who played the slap bass parts beyond King being the band's bassist. Echoes is dated 1984 on Wikipedia but other sources say 1983 or 1985.

culture.title: US number 7
culture.line: Released 13 September 1985, it reached 6 in the UK and 7 on the Hot 100, Level 42's only American top 10. It went gold in Canada.

culture.title: World Machine, 72 weeks
culture.line: The album, with Hafnarfjall in Iceland on the cover, reached 3 in the UK, stayed 72 weeks and had sold 2.5 million by 1987.
